opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think about this question quite a lot. Looking back, there's definitely a part of me that wonders "what if." Around the time I was finishing my PhD, the people who jumped directly into large-scale deep learning, into the labs that later became central to the generative AI wave, were in a position to shape something historic. I was close to that world, but my heart was in computer graphics, physical simulation, and programming languages. That's what Taichi grew out of.

Going to NVIDIA felt very natural at the time. It's a company that sits right at the intersection of graphics and computing. I learned an enormous amount about how real products are built, how hardware and software co-evolve, and how a big engineering organization thinks. Those lessons later became very valuable when I started my own company.

So do I regret it? I'd say no, but with an honest caveat. Every choice has an opportunity cost, and in hindsight the AI frontier moved faster and became bigger than almost anyone predicted, including me. If I had optimized purely for being where the biggest wave would be, maybe I would have chosen differently.

But I don't think life should be optimized only in hindsight. At that moment I chose based on what I genuinely loved and where I thought I could contribute something unique rather than being one more person in a crowded direction. I still believe that's a good principle. And the boundaries are blurring anyway. Simulation, 3D content, and AI are converging now, so the path I took isn't disconnected from the frontier. It's just a different entrance into it.

r001.rationale: He acknowledges that AI moved faster and that he might have chosen differently to be near the biggest wave, but he does not clearly judge that joining AI earlier would have benefited him more than joining NVIDIA. He says he does not regret his choice and values what he learned at NVIDIA.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't regret it. Everyone likes to look back and say, "If only I'd jumped into large models two years earlier," but that's hindsight talking. When I made that decision, the question in front of me wasn't "where will the AI frontier be in five years?" It was "where can I learn the most about the layer I care about, which is the hardware and the compiler stack underneath everything?"

At NVIDIA I got to see, up close, how a full system is actually built, from the silicon all the way up to the software people touch. That's not something you can read about in a paper. You have to sit inside it and watch how decisions get made, where the real bottlenecks are, why certain things that look easy on a whiteboard take an entire team a year. That understanding is exactly what I rely on now, because whatever happens on top of the models, the compute underneath is still the thing that determines what's possible.

So did I miss some early window? Maybe, in a narrow sense. But I think of it as taking a different path through the same mountain. People who went straight into models learned one set of things very deeply. I learned a different set, and now the two are converging. The frontier isn't a single door that closes behind you. It keeps reopening, and the people who can connect the systems side with the model side are the ones who end up useful when it does.

The one thing I'd tell my younger self is to be less anxious about timing. You can't optimize your career the way you optimize a kernel. You pick something you're genuinely curious about, you go deep, and you trust that depth compounds.

r001.rationale: He says he does not regret joining NVIDIA and describes its hardware and systems experience as valuable. He allows he may have missed an early window in a narrow sense, but does not say that participating earlier would have benefited him more.

astra-6.text: Looking back, I think it was a valuable choice. Of course, when you see how quickly AI has developed, it’s natural to wonder what would have happened if you’d joined that frontier earlier. But I wouldn’t judge the decision only by what became clear afterward. Working at NVIDIA gave me an opportunity to deepen my understanding of computing and the relationship between hardware and software. That’s relevant to AI, too. So there may have been an opportunity cost, but I don’t see that time as wasted. The more useful question is how to build on that experience and choose what to work on next.

r001.rationale: He acknowledges a possible opportunity cost of not joining AI earlier, but calls NVIDIA valuable and does not say earlier participation would have benefited him more.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, there was an opportunity cost. If I had focused on AI earlier, I might have participated more directly in some of those developments. But I don’t think that makes going to NVIDIA a mistake. At the time, it made sense for what I wanted to learn, and working on GPUs and high-performance computing gave me a foundation that is very relevant to AI today.

Of course, when you look backward, the winning direction always seems more obvious than it was. You have to distinguish between a decision that was reasonable with the information you had and a decision that looks optimal in hindsight. For me, the more useful question is what I should do with that experience now.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges that earlier AI focus might have enabled more direct participation, but it does not judge that as more beneficial than joining NVIDIA. It explicitly says going to NVIDIA was not a mistake and was useful preparation for AI.
